claim: S1PR3 KO mice displayed a dramatic loss of mechanical sensitivity with von Frey paw withdrawal thresholds significantly elevated (mean thresholds: 1.737 g vs. 0.736 and 0.610 g for WT and HET, respectively).
source: S1PR3 KO mice displayed a dramatic loss of mechanical sensitivity (Figure 1A; see Figure 1—source data 1), as von Frey paw withdrawal thresholds were significantly elevated in S1PR3 KO mice relative to WT and S1PR3 HET littermates (mean thresholds: 1.737 g vs. 0.736 and 0.610 g, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from von Frey testing shown in Figure 1A and quantified in the text.

claim: S1PR3 KO mice demonstrated decreased responses to noxious tactile stimuli (2–6 g) but normal responsiveness to innocuous tactile stimuli (0.6–1.4 g).
source: Moreover, S1PR3 KO mice demonstrated decreased responses to a range of noxious tactile stimuli (2–6 g; Figure 1B) and to noxious pinprick stimulation (Figure 1C), but normal responsiveness to innocuous tactile stimuli (0.6–1.4 g; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from force-response measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: S1PR3 KO mice exhibited normal tape removal attempts.
source: S1PR3 KO mice exhibited normal tape removal attempts (Ranade et al., 2014) (Figure 1D), righting reflexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), radiant heat withdrawal latencies (Figure 1E), and itch-evoked scratching (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the tape assay shown in Figure 1D and cited reference.

claim: S1PR3 KO mice exhibited normal righting reflexes.
source: S1PR3 KO mice exhibited normal tape removal attempts (Ranade et al., 2014) (Figure 1D), righting reflexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), radiant heat withdrawal latencies (Figure 1E), and itch-evoked scratching (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from righting reflex measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: S1PR3 KO mice exhibited normal radiant heat withdrawal latencies.
source: S1PR3 KO mice exhibited normal tape removal attempts (Ranade et al., 2014) (Figure 1D), righting reflexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), radiant heat withdrawal latencies (Figure 1E), and itch-evoked scratching (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radiant heat testing shown in Figure 1E.

claim: S1PR3 KO mice exhibited normal itch-evoked scratching.
source: S1PR3 KO mice exhibited normal tape removal attempts (Ranade et al., 2014) (Figure 1D), righting reflexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), radiant heat withdrawal latencies (Figure 1E), and itch-evoked scratching (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from itch behavior testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Intradermal injection of 500 µM TY 52156 (S1PR3-selective antagonist) into the mouse hindpaw triggered a rapid and significant elevation in von Frey paw withdrawal thresholds.
source: Similar to the phenotype of knockout animals, intradermal injection of 500 µM TY into the mouse hindpaw (the site of testing) triggered a rapid and significant elevation in von Frey paw withdrawal thresholds (Figure 1F) and decreased responsiveness to noxious (2–6 g), but not innocuous (0.6–1.4 g), tactile stimuli (Figure 1G), without affecting noxious heat sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological blockade experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: TY 52156 injection decreased responsiveness to noxious (2–6 g), but not innocuous (0.6–1.4 g), tactile stimuli.
source: Similar to the phenotype of knockout animals, intradermal injection of 500 µM TY into the mouse hindpaw (the site of testing) triggered a rapid and significant elevation in von Frey paw withdrawal thresholds (Figure 1F) and decreased responsiveness to noxious (2–6 g), but not innocuous (0.6–1.4 g), tactile stimuli (Figure 1G), without affecting noxious heat sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from force-response measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: TY 52156 injection did not affect noxious heat sensitivity.
source: Similar to the phenotype of knockout animals, intradermal injection of 500 µM TY into the mouse hindpaw (the site of testing) triggered a rapid and significant elevation in von Frey paw withdrawal thresholds (Figure 1F) and decreased responsiveness to noxious (2–6 g), but not innocuous (0.6–1.4 g), tactile stimuli (Figure 1G), without affecting noxious heat sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radiant heat testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Blockade of S1PR1 with the selective antagonist W146 had no effect on baseline mechanical or thermal thresholds.
source: By contrast, blockade of S1PR1 with the selective antagonist W146 (Finley et al., 2013) had no effect on baseline mechanical or thermal thresholds (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological blockade experiments shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, and cited reference.

claim: Decreasing local S1P levels with SKI II significantly reduced mechanical sensitivity.
source: Decreasing local S1P levels with SKI II significantly reduced mechanical sensitivity (Figure 2A; see Figure 2—source data 1), comparable to the hyposensitivity phenotype observed in S1PR3 KO mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SKI II injection experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Peripheral blockade of S1P production had no effect on baseline thermal sensitivity.
source: Again, similar to what was observed in S1PR3 KO animals (Figure 1E), peripheral blockade of S1P production had no effect on baseline thermal sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radiant heat testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Injecting exogenous S1P (10 µM) had no effect on mechanical sensitivity.
source: Surprisingly, injecting exogenous S1P (10 µM; maximum solubility in saline vehicle) had no effect on mechanical sensitivity (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from S1P injection experiments shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: S1P injection triggered S1PR3-dependent thermal hypersensitivity and spontaneous pain.
source: However, as previously reported (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013), S1P injection triggered S1PR3-dependent thermal hypersensitivity and spontaneous pain (Figure 2C–D), demonstrating that the lack of effect on mechanical hypersensitivity is not due to problems with S1P delivery or degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D and cited references.

claim: Injection of exogenous S1P reversed SKI II-induced mechanical hyposensitivity in a dose-dependent manner, with maximal effect at 200 nM S1P.
source: Indeed, we found that injection of exogenous S1P reversed SKI II-induced mechanical hyposensitivity in a dose-dependent manner, and observed a maximal effect with 200 nM S1P (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from S1P rescue experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 43% of cells from wild-type DRG expressed S1pr3.
source: In our experiments, 43% of cells from wild-type DRG expressed S1pr3.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data quantifying S1pr3 expression.

claim: 39.9% of all S1pr3+ cells expressed Scn1a.
source: These cells expressed Scn1a (39.9% of all S1pr3+), a gene that encodes the Nav1.1 sodium channel, which mediates mechanical pain in Aδ fibers (Osteen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-ISH data and cited reference.

claim: 20.4% of all S1pr3+ cells expressed Npy2r.
source: S1pr3+ cells also co-expressed Npy2r (20.4% of all S1pr3+), a marker of a subset of mechanonociceptive A fibers (Arcourt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-ISH data and cited reference.

claim: S1pr3 was expressed in 70.6% of Scn1a+ cells.
source: S1pr3 was expressed in 70.6% of Scn1a+ cells and 72% of Npy2r+ cells, comprising a majority of both of these populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-ISH data.

claim: S1pr3 was expressed in 72% of Npy2r+ cells.
source: S1pr3 was expressed in 70.6% of Scn1a+ cells and 72% of Npy2r+ cells, comprising a majority of both of these populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-ISH data.

claim: 67.1% of all S1pr3+ cells were Trpv1+ and/or Trpa1+ C nociceptors.
source: The remaining S1pr3+ cells were Trpv1+ and/or Trpa1+ C nociceptors (67.1% of all S1pr3+), which are reported to overlap minimally with the Scn1a+ and Npy2r+ populations (Arcourt et al., 2017; Osteen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-ISH data and cited references.

claim: 42.4% of S1PR3+ cells co-stained with anti-Peripherin.
source: We found that 42.4% of S1PR3+ cells co-stained with anti-Peripherin, demonstrating that S1PR3 is expressed in a subset of small-diameter neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data from S1pr3mCherry/+ reporter mice.

claim: 69.5% of S1PR3+ cells co-stained with anti-NF200.
source: We also observed that 69.5% of S1PR3+ cells co-stained with anti-NF200, which marks medium and large-diameter myelinated neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data from S1pr3mCherry/+ reporter mice.

claim: S1PR3+ cells were primarily of small to medium diameter (11.3–35.1 µm).
source: Furthermore, we observed that S1PR3+ cells were primarily of small to medium diameter (11.3–35.1 µm), whereas all cells in the DRG ranged from 11.3 to 53.9 µm.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell diameter measurements from IHC data.

claim: Only 56.1 ± 22.4% of mCherry-expressing neurons were activated by 1 µM S1P.
source: Interestingly, only 56.1 ± 22.4% of mCherry-expressing neurons were activated by 1 µM S1P (Representative trace in Figure 4B; representative images in Figure 4C), which our dose-response showed to be the saturating concentration for calcium influx (Figure 4D; EC50 = 155 nM).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: All S1P-responsive neurons were also capsaicin-sensitive (n > 2000 neurons).
source: All S1P-responsive neurons were also capsaicin-sensitive (n > 2000 neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data from over 2000 neurons.

claim: The mean diameter of S1P-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 22.4 ± 1.0 µm.
source: The mean diameter of S1P-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 22.4 ± 1.0 µm, whereas the mean diameter of non-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 28.7 ± 3.2 µm (p=0.0002, two-tailed t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell diameter measurements from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The mean diameter of non-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 28.7 ± 3.2 µm.
source: The mean diameter of S1P-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 22.4 ± 1.0 µm, whereas the mean diameter of non-responsive mCherry+ neurons was 28.7 ± 3.2 µm (p=0.0002, two-tailed t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell diameter measurements from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: S1P evoked action potential firing in capsaicin-sensitive small diameter cells.
source: We also performed whole cell current clamp experiments and, consistent with other studies (Mair et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015), found that S1P evoked action potential firing in capsaicin-sensitive small diameter cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4E and cited references.

claim: 44.2 ± 15.1% of Hm1a-responsive neurons expressed mCherry.
source: Indeed, we found that 44.2 ± 15.1% of Hm1a-responsive neurons expressed mCherry (Figure 4F), consistent with our staining showing expression of S1pr3 in AM nociceptors and the role of Hm1a-responsive neurons in mediating mechanical pain in vivo (Osteen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4F and cited reference.

claim: S1P dramatically lowered the threshold to fire action potentials (rheobase) in an S1PR3-dependent manner.
source: However, S1P dramatically lowered the threshold to fire action potentials (rheobase) in an S1PR3-dependent manner (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: S1P triggered a robust increase in input resistance.
source: By contrast, S1P triggered a robust increase in input resistance (Figure 5B), consistent with the closure of potassium channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The current inhibited by S1P application was carried by potassium.
source: I-V analysis revealed that the current inhibited by S1P application was carried by potassium (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by I-V analysis data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: S1P significantly reduced slow, voltage-dependent tail current amplitudes in an S1PR3-dependent manner.
source: Additionally, S1P significantly reduced slow, voltage-dependent tail current amplitudes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F; Figure 5D (top)) in an S1PR3-dependent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, center).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The KCNQ2/3-selective inhibitor XE 991 completely occluded the effects of S1P on tail current.
source: To address whether KCNQ2/3 channels mediated S1P-dependent neuronal excitability, we applied the KCNQ2/3-selective inhibitor XE 991 and found that it completely occluded the effects of S1P on tail current (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Linopirdine occluded the effects of S1P on tail current.
source: Similar results were observed with the related antagonist, linopirdine (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The effect of S1P on KCNQ2/3 currents exhibited an IC50 of 48 nM with saturation at 100 nM.
source: We also found that the effect of S1P on KCNQ2/3 currents was mediated by low levels of S1P, exhibiting an IC50 of 48 nM with saturation at 100 nM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: S1PR3 KO AM nociceptors displayed reduced sensitivity in their force-response relation (slope for HET versus KO: 50 Hz/N versus 35 Hz/N).
source: Compared to S1PR3 HET, S1PR3 KO AM nociceptors displayed reduced sensitivity in their force-response relation (slope for HET versus KO: 50 Hz/N versus 35 Hz/N), as well as attenuated firing over the noxious, but not innocuous, range of mechanical stimulation (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The median von Frey threshold to elicit firing in AM nociceptors was significantly higher in S1PR3 KO animals (3.92 mN) compared to littermate controls (1.56 mN).
source: Strikingly, the median von Frey threshold to elicit firing in AM nociceptors was significantly higher in S1PR3 KO animals (3.92 mN) compared to littermate controls (1.56 mN; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: S1PR3 KO AM nociceptors displayed a right-shifted cumulative response curve to force-controlled stimuli (50% effective force for HET versus KO: 33.7 versus 60.0 mN).
source: Furthermore, S1PR3 KO AM nociceptors displayed a right-shifted cumulative response curve to force-controlled stimuli (50% effective force for HET versus KO: 33.7 versus 60.0 mN; Figure 6C), consistent with the mechanonociceptive hyposensitivity observed in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Neither AM conduction velocities nor the conduction velocity distributions of Aβ, Aδ, and C fibers differed between genotypes.
source: By contrast, neither AM conduction velocities nor the conduction velocity distributions of Aβ, Aδ, and C fibers differed between genotypes (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by conduction velocity measurements shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: S1PR3 KO animals displayed a significantly lower proportion of Adapting AM nociceptors compared with littermate controls.
source: S1PR3 KO animals displayed a significantly lower proportion of Adapting AM nociceptors compared with littermate controls (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: S1PR3 KO mice failed to develop thermal hypersensitivity relative to heterozygous littermates at both 24 and 48 hr post-CFA injection.
source: Strikingly, S1PR3 KO mice failed to develop thermal hypersensitivity (Figure 7A; see Figure 7—source data 1) relative to heterozygous littermates at both 24 and 48 hr post-CFA injection.
evidence: The claim is supported by CFA inflammatory pain model data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: S1PR3 KO animals developed robust mechanical hypersensitivity when thresholds were normalized to account for baseline differences.
source: In stark contrast, S1PR3 KO animals developed robust mechanical hypersensitivity when thresholds were normalized to account for the dramatic baseline differences between knockouts and control animals (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFA inflammatory pain model data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Flow cytometry experiments showed robust infiltration of immune cells into hindpaw skin from both S1PR3 KO and littermate controls.
source: Consistent with the development of mechanical hypersensitivity, flow cytometry experiments showed robust infiltration of immune cells into hindpaw skin from both S1PR3 KO and littermate controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Acute blockade of S1P production with SKI II reversed CFA heat hypersensitivity.
source: Acute blockade of S1P production with SKI II or S1PR3 with TY also reversed CFA heat hypersensitivity (Figure 7C), demonstrating that peripheral S1P actively signals via S1PR3 to promote CFA-evoked heat hypersensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological blockade data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Acute blockade of S1PR3 with TY reversed CFA heat hypersensitivity.
source: Acute blockade of S1P production with SKI II or S1PR3 with TY also reversed CFA heat hypersensitivity (Figure 7C), demonstrating that peripheral S1P actively signals via S1PR3 to promote CFA-evoked heat hypersensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological blockade data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Acute S1P/S1PR3 blockade with SKI II or TY elevated mechanical thresholds to pre-CFA, baseline levels.
source: Furthermore, acute S1P/S1PR3 blockade with SKI II or TY elevated mechanical thresholds to pre-CFA, baseline levels (Figure 7D) showing that S1PR3 tunes mechanical pain under normal and inflammatory conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological blockade data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: S1P signaling via S1PR3 is a key pathway that tunes mechanical pain sensitivity.
source: We now show that S1P signaling via S1PR3 is a key pathway that tunes mechanical pain sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: S1P/S1PR3 sets baseline mechanical pain thresholds.
source: First, S1P/S1PR3 sets baseline mechanical pain thresholds.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by behavioral and electrophysiological data.

claim: Depletion of baseline, endogenous S1P induces mechanical hyposensitivity.
source: Depletion of baseline, endogenous S1P induces mechanical hyposensitivity and nanomolar levels of exogenous S1P are sufficient to restore normal mechanical pain sensitivity after depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by SKI II injection experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Nanomolar levels of exogenous S1P are sufficient to restore normal mechanical pain sensitivity after depletion.
source: Depletion of baseline, endogenous S1P induces mechanical hyposensitivity and nanomolar levels of exogenous S1P are sufficient to restore normal mechanical pain sensitivity after depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by S1P rescue experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Elevated micromolar S1P levels promote thermal, but not mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: Second, elevated micromolar S1P levels, such as those produced during inflammation or disease, promote thermal, but not mechanical hypersensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by S1P injection experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The effects of S1P on acute mechanical pain and thermal hypersensitivity are completely lost in S1PR3 knockout animals.
source: The effects of S1P on acute mechanical pain and thermal hypersensitivity are completely lost in S1PR3 knockout animals, which are otherwise normal with respect to other somatosensory behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from S1PR3 KO mice shown in Figures 1 and 7.

claim: S1PR3 is indispensable for normal function of AM nociceptors, including the adapting AM population.
source: Our study demonstrates that S1PR3 is indispensable for normal function of AM nociceptors, including the adapting AM population, recently discussed in Arcourt et al., that innervates the epidermis and encodes noxious touch (Arcourt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6 and cited reference.

claim: S1PR3 signaling modulates KCNQ2/3 channels to regulate excitability of A mechanonociceptors.
source: We show that S1PR3 signaling modulates KCNQ2/3 channels to regulate excitability of these A mechanonociceptors (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5 and summarized in Figure 8.

claim: KCNQ channels mediate excitability of Aδ fibers.
source: Other studies have shown that KCNQ channels mediate excitability of Aδ fibers (Schütze et al., 2016; Passmore et al., 2012) and are required for normal mechanonociceptive responses in dorsal horn neurons receiving Aδ input (Passmore et al., 2012), and that opening KCNQ2/3 channels directly with retigabine alleviates pain in vivo (Xu et al., 2010; Hayashi et al., 2014; Blackburn-Munro and Jensen, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Opening KCNQ2/3 channels directly with retigabine alleviates pain in vivo.
source: Other studies have shown that KCNQ channels mediate excitability of Aδ fibers (Schütze et al., 2016; Passmore et al., 2012) and are required for normal mechanonociceptive responses in dorsal horn neurons receiving Aδ input (Passmore et al., 2012), and that opening KCNQ2/3 channels directly with retigabine alleviates pain in vivo (Xu et al., 2010; Hayashi et al., 2014; Blackburn-Munro and Jensen, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: S1pr3 and Kcnq2/3 are highly expressed in human sensory ganglia.
source: Finally, S1pr3 and Kcnq2/3 are highly expressed in human sensory ganglia (Ray et al., 2018; Flegel et al., 2015) and recordings from human stem cell-derived sensory neurons show that KCNQ2/3 channels play a key role in mediating their excitability (Young et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Recordings from human stem cell-derived sensory neurons show that KCNQ2/3 channels play a key role in mediating their excitability.
source: Finally, S1pr3 and Kcnq2/3 are highly expressed in human sensory ganglia (Ray et al., 2018; Flegel et al., 2015) and recordings from human stem cell-derived sensory neurons show that KCNQ2/3 channels play a key role in mediating their excitability (Young et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: Thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model is dependent on TRPV1 ion channels.
source: For example, thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model is dependent on TRPV1 ion channels (Caterina et al., 2000) and independent of immune cell infiltration (Ghasemlou et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model is independent of immune cell infiltration.
source: For example, thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model is dependent on TRPV1 ion channels (Caterina et al., 2000) and independent of immune cell infiltration (Ghasemlou et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: Infiltration of a subset of myeloid immune cells is required for mechanical hypersensitivity in an inflammatory pain model.
source: By contrast, infiltration of a subset of myeloid immune cells is required for mechanical hypersensitivity in an inflammatory pain model (Ghasemlou et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: S1P is a key component of the inflammatory soup that triggers thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model.
source: Here we show that S1P via S1PR3 signaling is a key component of the inflammatory soup that triggers thermal hypersensitivity in the CFA model.
evidence: The claim is supported by CFA model data shown in Figure 7.

claim: S1P signaling via S1PR1 allows for the continuous circulation of lymphocytes between blood, lymph, and peripheral tissues.
source: Outside of the nervous system, S1P signaling via S1PR1 allows for the continuous circulation of lymphocytes between blood, lymph, and peripheral tissues (Matloubian et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: Fingolimod is prescribed as an immunosuppressant for multiple sclerosis treatment.
source: Indeed, fingolimod, a non-selective S1PR modulator, is prescribed as an immunosuppressant for multiple sclerosis treatment (Brinkmann et al., 2010), but the possibility that some of its therapeutic effects may also be mediated via the nervous system has not been fully explored.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference and established medical knowledge.

claim: Intrathecal fingolimod reduces bone cancer pain.
source: Likewise, one study found that intrathecal fingolimod reduces bone cancer pain (Grenald et al., 2017), and while analgesia was attributed to effects on S1PR1 in glia, some of the benefits may be due to S1PR3 signaling in DRG neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: Thermal pain is detected by thermosensitive TRP channels in subsets of nociceptors.
source: Thermal pain is detected by thermosensitive TRP channels in subsets of nociceptors (Caterina et al., 2000; Vriens et al., 2011), and gentle touch is detected by Piezo2 channels in low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs) (Ranade et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Gentle touch is detected by Piezo2 channels in low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs).
source: Thermal pain is detected by thermosensitive TRP channels in subsets of nociceptors (Caterina et al., 2000; Vriens et al., 2011), and gentle touch is detected by Piezo2 channels in low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs) (Ranade et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Aδ high-threshold mechanoreceptors (HTMRs) play a key role in responses to painful mechanical stimuli.
source: Aδ high-threshold mechanoreceptors (HTMRs) have been shown to play a key role in responses to painful mechanical stimuli (Arcourt et al., 2017; Ghitani et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: The Npy2r+ subpopulation of HTMRs mediates fast paw withdrawal responses to pinprick stimulation and terminates as free nerve endings in the epidermis.
source: The Npy2r+ subpopulation of HTMRs mediates fast paw withdrawal responses to pinprick stimulation and terminates as free nerve endings in the epidermis (Arcourt et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: The Calca+ subpopulation of circumferential-HTMRs responds to noxious force and hair pulling, and terminates as circumferential endings wrapped around guard hair follicles.
source: The Calca+ subpopulation of circumferential-HTMRs responds to noxious force and hair pulling, and terminates as circumferential endings wrapped around guard hair follicles (Ghitani et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing interneurons of laminae I-III in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord receive input from nociceptors and are required for behavioral responses to painful mechanical stimuli.
source: Additionally, somatostatin-expressing interneurons of laminae I-III in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord receive input from nociceptors and are required for behavioral responses to painful mechanical stimuli (Duan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: S1P is a bioactive lipid that signals via 5 G-protein coupled S1P Receptors (S1PRs 1–5).
source: S1P is a bioactive lipid that signals via 5 G-protein coupled S1P Receptors (S1PRs 1–5).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of S1P signaling.

claim: S1P signaling, mainly via S1PR1, plays a well-known role in immune cell migration and maturation.
source: S1P signaling, mainly via S1PR1, plays a well-known role in immune cell migration and maturation (Spiegel and Milstien, 2003; Matloubian et al., 2004; Schwab et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: S1PRs are expressed throughout the nervous system.
source: Additionally, recent studies have shown that S1PRs are expressed throughout the nervous system (Janes et al., 2014; Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013) and S1P signaling is associated with a variety of neuroinflammatory disorders, including multiple sclerosis (Brinkmann et al., 2010) and Alzheimer's disease (Couttas et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: S1P signaling is associated with multiple sclerosis.
source: Additionally, recent studies have shown that S1PRs are expressed throughout the nervous system (Janes et al., 2014; Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013) and S1P signaling is associated with a variety of neuroinflammatory disorders, including multiple sclerosis (Brinkmann et al., 2010) and Alzheimer's disease (Couttas et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: S1P signaling is associated with Alzheimer's disease.
source: Additionally, recent studies have shown that S1PRs are expressed throughout the nervous system (Janes et al., 2014; Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013) and S1P signaling is associated with a variety of neuroinflammatory disorders, including multiple sclerosis (Brinkmann et al., 2010) and Alzheimer's disease (Couttas et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: S1P has been implicated in spontaneous pain.
source: S1P has been implicated in spontaneous pain (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013) and thermal pain hypersensitivity (Mair et al., 2011; Finley et al., 2013; Weth et al., 2015), but due to conflicting accounts of S1P receptor expression in the CNS (Janes et al., 2014; Weth-Malsch et al., 2016) and PNS (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Usoskin et al., 2015) as well as inconsistent reports on the effects of S1P on neuronal excitability (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015) and pain behaviors (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Finley et al., 2013; Weth et al., 2015), the role of S1P in somatosensation remains controversial.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: S1P has been implicated in thermal pain hypersensitivity.
source: S1P has been implicated in spontaneous pain (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013) and thermal pain hypersensitivity (Mair et al., 2011; Finley et al., 2013; Weth et al., 2015), but due to conflicting accounts of S1P receptor expression in the CNS (Janes et al., 2014; Weth-Malsch et al., 2016) and PNS (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Usoskin et al., 2015) as well as inconsistent reports on the effects of S1P on neuronal excitability (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015) and pain behaviors (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Finley et al., 2013; Weth et al., 2015), the role of S1P in somatosensation remains controversial.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Transcriptome analysis of the sensory ganglia innervating the tactile organ of the star-nosed mole revealed enrichment of several components of the S1P pathway, including S1pr3.
source: To identify candidate genes underlying mechanosensation, we previously performed transcriptome analysis of the sensory ganglia innervating the ultra-sensitive tactile organ (the star) of the star-nosed mole (Gerhold et al., 2013). Immunostaining revealed the tactile organ is preferentially innervated by myelinated Aδ fibers (Gerhold et al., 2013), which are primarily mechanosensitive. While our original analysis focused on ion channels enriched in the neurons of the star organ, our dataset also revealed enrichment of several components of the S1P pathway, including S1pr3.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis data and cited reference.

claim: Single-cell RNA seq of mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons revealed S1pr3 expression in a subset of myelinated mechanoreceptors and a subpopulation of peptidergic C nociceptors.
source: Likewise, single-cell RNA seq of mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons revealed S1pr3 expression in a subset of myelinated mechanoreceptors (Usoskin et al., 2015) in addition to a subpopulation of peptidergic C nociceptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA seq data and cited reference.

claim: S1P promotes excitability in small-diameter, capsaicin-sensitive nociceptors.
source: S1P promotes excitability in small-diameter, capsaicin-sensitive nociceptors (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2006; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: S1PR3 has been shown to mediate spontaneous pain triggered by elevated S1P and thermal sensitization following sterile tissue injury.
source: In addition, S1PR3 has been shown to mediate spontaneous pain triggered by elevated S1P and thermal sensitization following sterile tissue injury (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: S1P application did not change membrane potential in medium-diameter S1pr3mCherry/+ dissociated DRG neurons.
source: In these cells, 1 µM S1P application did not change membrane potential (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; see Figure 5—source data 1) or elicit firing in the absence of current injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: S1P did not elicit firing in the absence of current injection in medium-diameter S1pr3mCherry/+ dissociated DRG neurons.
source: In these cells, 1 µM S1P application did not change membrane potential (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; see Figure 5—source data 1) or elicit firing in the absence of current injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5A.

claim: S1P had no effect on voltage-gated sodium currents in S1PR3+ medium-diameter cells.
source: We found that S1P had no such effects on S1PR3+ medium-diameter cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: S1P had no effect on steady-state potassium currents in S1PR3+ medium-diameter cells.
source: We found that S1P had no such effects on S1PR3+ medium-diameter cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Tail currents in Aδ neurons are primarily mediated by KCNQ2/3 potassium channels.
source: As tail currents in Aδ neurons are primarily mediated by KCNQ2/3 potassium channels (Schütze et al., 2016; Passmore et al., 2012), we postulated that S1P may alter tail currents through modulation of these channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Under normal conditions, AM nociceptors set mechanical pain thresholds.
source: Under normal conditions, AM nociceptors set mechanical pain thresholds (Osteen et al., 2016; Abrahamsen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Under inflammatory conditions, the combined activity of both non-sensitized AM fibers and sensitized C fibers determines overall post-inflammatory mechanical thresholds.
source: By contrast, under inflammatory conditions, the combined activity of both non-sensitized AM fibers and sensitized C fibers determines overall post-inflammatory mechanical thresholds (Lennertz et al., 2012; Abrahamsen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: All cells in the body, including somatosensory neurons, immune cells, and skin cells, express sphingosine kinases 1 and 2 which are essential for S1P production.
source: All cells in the body, including somatosensory neurons, immune cells, and skin cells, express sphingosine kinases 1 and 2 which are essential for S1P production (Chalfant and Spiegel, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: Deletion of both sphingosine kinases is lethal.
source: Deletion of both kinases is lethal and attempts to conditionally knockout these kinases fail to completely eliminate S1P in tissues (Pappu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: Attempts to conditionally knockout sphingosine kinases fail to completely eliminate S1P in tissues.
source: Deletion of both kinases is lethal and attempts to conditionally knockout these kinases fail to completely eliminate S1P in tissues (Pappu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: RNA seq data suggests that somatosensory neurons contain all of the enzymatic machinery required to produce and export local S1P.
source: While RNA seq data suggests that somatosensory neurons contain all of the enzymatic machinery required to produce and export local S1P (Usoskin et al., 2015; Morita et al., 2015), future work will be needed to identify the key cell types that are important for maintaining baseline S1P levels in the skin to regulate mechanical sensitivity and for increasing S1P under inflammatory/injury conditions to promote pain hypersensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA seq data and cited references.

claim: Piezo2-hypomorphic animals exhibit normal mechanical pain behaviors.
source: For example, although Piezo2-hypomorphic animals exhibit normal mechanical pain behaviors (Ranade et al., 2014), ex vivo skin-nerve recordings show that their AM nociceptors display decreased force-responsiveness (Ranade et al., 2014), and a recent study found that subpopulations of sensory neurons express different splice variants of Piezo2 that exhibit different force sensitivities (Szczot et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: Ex vivo skin-nerve recordings show that AM nociceptors in Piezo2-hypomorphic animals display decreased force-responsiveness.
source: For example, although Piezo2-hypomorphic animals exhibit normal mechanical pain behaviors (Ranade et al., 2014), ex vivo skin-nerve recordings show that their AM nociceptors display decreased force-responsiveness (Ranade et al., 2014), and a recent study found that subpopulations of sensory neurons express different splice variants of Piezo2 that exhibit different force sensitivities (Szczot et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: Subpopulations of sensory neurons express different splice variants of Piezo2 that exhibit different force sensitivities.
source: For example, although Piezo2-hypomorphic animals exhibit normal mechanical pain behaviors (Ranade et al., 2014), ex vivo skin-nerve recordings show that their AM nociceptors display decreased force-responsiveness (Ranade et al., 2014), and a recent study found that subpopulations of sensory neurons express different splice variants of Piezo2 that exhibit different force sensitivities (Szczot et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: The neurons that innervate the ultra-sensitive tactile organ of the star-nosed mole are highly enriched in transcripts for S1PR3 and KCNQ channels.
source: Interestingly, the neurons that innervate the ultra-sensitive tactile organ of the star-nosed mole are highly enriched in transcripts for S1PR3 and KCNQ channels, as well as for a variety of other potassium channels (Gerhold et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis data and cited reference.

claim: Single-cell RNA seq datasets from mouse DRG neurons show co-expression of S1pr3 and Kcnq2/3 in a subset of myelinated mechanoreceptors.
source: Moreover, the link between S1pr3 and Kcnq2/3 is echoed in single-cell RNA seq datasets from mouse DRG neurons, which show co-expression of S1pr3 and Kcnq2/3 in a subset of myelinated mechanoreceptors (Usoskin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA seq data and cited reference.

claim: S1P has been linked to a wide range of human inflammatory disorders.
source: S1P has been linked to a wide range of human inflammatory disorders (Allende et al., 2011; Kunkel et al., 2013; Roviezzo et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2013; Rivera et al., 2008; Myśliwiec et al., 2017; Checa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: S1P signaling via S1PR1 is thought to promote inflammation via the immune system.
source: Canonically, S1P signaling via S1PR1 is thought to promote inflammation via the immune system (Kunkel et al., 2013), however, we propose that S1P signaling via S1PR3 in neurons may also contribute to inflammatory disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: S1PR3-expressing somatosensory neurons contribute to neurogenic inflammation in asthma.
source: S1PR3 inhibitors may also be beneficial for treating other inflammatory disorders where S1PR3-expressing somatosensory neurons have been shown to contribute to neurogenic inflammation, such as asthma (Tränkner et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: 48.3% of neurons from adult reporter animals expressed S1PR3-mCherry fusion protein.
source: Live imaging of cultured DRG neurons from adult reporter animals showed expression of S1PR3-mCherry fusion protein in 48.3% of neurons, mirroring our ISH and IHC results (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The EC50 for S1P-induced calcium influx is 155 nM.
source: Interestingly, only 56.1 ± 22.4% of mCherry-expressing neurons were activated by 1 µM S1P (Representative trace in Figure 4B; representative images in Figure 4C), which our dose-response showed to be the saturating concentration for calcium influx (Figure 4D; EC50 = 155 nM).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Sensory neurons from S1PR3 KO animals did not respond to S1P.
source: And while sensory neurons from S1PR3 KO animals did not respond to S1P, as expected (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013), they exhibited capsaicin responses that were not significantly different from WT neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and cited reference.

claim: S1PR3 KO neurons exhibited capsaicin responses that were not significantly different from WT neurons.
source: And while sensory neurons from S1PR3 KO animals did not respond to S1P, as expected (Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013), they exhibited capsaicin responses that were not significantly different from WT neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: No significant differences were observed between WT and S1PR3 KO DRG in number of Trpa1+, Trpv1+, Peripherin+, NF200+, or IB4+ cells.
source: Additionally, no significant differences were observed between WT and S1PR3 KO DRG in number of Trpa1+, Trpv1+, Peripherin+, NF200+, or IB4+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C,F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH and IHC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C,F,G.

claim: The mean diameters of Trpv1+ neurons in WT versus KO DRG were not significantly different.
source: The mean diameters of Trpv1+ neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, left), NF200+ neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), or all neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, right) in WT versus KO DRG were not significantly different, suggesting no loss of major sensory neuronal subtypes in the S1PR3 KO.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell diameter measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The mean diameters of NF200+ neurons in WT versus KO DRG were not significantly different.
source: The mean diameters of Trpv1+ neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, left), NF200+ neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), or all neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, right) in WT versus KO DRG were not significantly different, suggesting no loss of major sensory neuronal subtypes in the S1PR3 KO.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell diameter measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The mean diameters of all neurons in WT versus KO DRG were not significantly different.
source: The mean diameters of Trpv1+ neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, left), NF200+ neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), or all neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, right) in WT versus KO DRG were not significantly different, suggesting no loss of major sensory neuronal subtypes in the S1PR3 KO.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell diameter measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: S1PR3 is not expressed in NF200+ circumferential or lanceolate hair follicle receptors.
source: We observed overlap of S1PR3-expressing free nerve endings with NF200+ myelinated free nerves and NF200- putative C-fiber endings (Figure 3F), but did not observe expression of S1PR3 in NF200+ circumferential or lanceolate hair follicle receptors, or in putative Merkel afferents (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: S1PR3 is not expressed in putative Merkel afferents.
source: We observed overlap of S1PR3-expressing free nerve endings with NF200+ myelinated free nerves and NF200- putative C-fiber endings (Figure 3F), but did not observe expression of S1PR3 in NF200+ circumferential or lanceolate hair follicle receptors, or in putative Merkel afferents (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: β-tubulin III, PGP9.5, and NF200 staining in S1PR3 KO skin displayed patterns of epidermal and dermal innervation similar to WT skin.
source: β-tubulin III, PGP9.5 (pan-neuronal markers), and NF200 staining in S1PR3 KO skin displayed patterns of epidermal and dermal innervation similar to WT skin, suggesting the phenotypes observed in the S1PR3 KO mice are not due to developmental loss of sensory neuronal innervation (pPGP9.5= 0.443 (n = 93, 38 fibers); pNefH = 0.405 (n = 61, 28 fibers); pBTIII = 0.353 (n = 104, 89 fibers); two-tailed t-tests based on average number of fibers per field of view).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data and statistical analysis.

claim: S1PR3 is expressed in subsets of myelinated A mechanonociceptors and unmyelinated C nociceptors that terminate as free nerve endings.
source: These results support expression of S1PR3 in subsets of myelinated A mechanonociceptors and unmyelinated C nociceptors that terminate as free nerve endings.
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data from skin and DRG.

claim: S1PR3 KO AM fibers displayed attenuated firing over the noxious, but not innocuous, range of mechanical stimulation.
source: Compared to S1PR3 HET, S1PR3 KO AM nociceptors displayed reduced sensitivity in their force-response relation (slope for HET versus KO: 50 Hz/N versus 35 Hz/N), as well as attenuated firing over the noxious, but not innocuous, range of mechanical stimulation (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: S1PR3 KO animals displayed an increase in AM fibers that were unresponsive to controlled force stimulation.
source: Additionally, we observed an increase in S1PR3 KO AM fibers that were unresponsive to controlled force stimulation (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The Non-adapting AMs and the few remaining mechanosensitive Adapting AMs in the S1PR3 KO displayed similar firing frequencies over both the dynamic and static phases of force application to control fibers.
source: The Non-adapting AMs, and the few remaining mechanosensitive Adapting AMs in the S1PR3 KO displayed similar firing frequencies over both the dynamic and static phases of force application to control fibers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Decreased mechanosensitivity of the Adapting AM population accounts for the significant reduction in force-firing relations observed at the population level in S1PR3 KO AMs.
source: This suggests that decreased mechanosensitivity of the Adapting AM population accounts for the significant reduction in force-firing relations observed at the population level in S1PR3 KO AMs (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on ex vivo skin-nerve recording data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: S1PR3 is an essential regulator of both mechanical threshold and sensitivity in a distinct population of AM nociceptors.
source: We conclude that S1PR3 is an essential regulator of both mechanical threshold and sensitivity in a distinct population of AM nociceptors.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on ex vivo skin-nerve recording data.

claim: S1PR3 mediates baseline mechanical sensitivity and is not required for the development of CFA-evoked mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: Our data demonstrate that S1PR3 mediates baseline mechanical sensitivity and is not required for the development of CFA-evoked mechanical hypersensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by CFA inflammatory pain model data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Peripheral S1P actively signals via S1PR3 to promote CFA-evoked heat hypersensitivity.
source: Acute blockade of S1P production with SKI II or S1PR3 with TY also reversed CFA heat hypersensitivity (Figure 7C), demonstrating that peripheral S1P actively signals via S1PR3 to promote CFA-evoked heat hypersensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological blockade data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: S1PR3 tunes mechanical pain under normal and inflammatory conditions.
source: Furthermore, acute S1P/S1PR3 blockade with SKI II or TY elevated mechanical thresholds to pre-CFA, baseline levels (Figure 7D) showing that S1PR3 tunes mechanical pain under normal and inflammatory conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological blockade data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Acute blockade of S1P production or S1PR3 activity under normal conditions induces mechanical hyposensitivity.
source: Consistent with this model, acute blockade of S1P production or S1PR3 activity under normal conditions induces mechanical hyposensitivity and under inflammatory conditions returns mechanical sensitivity to normal levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological blockade data shown in Figures 1 and 7.

claim: Acute blockade of S1P production or S1PR3 activity under inflammatory conditions returns mechanical sensitivity to normal levels.
source: Consistent with this model, acute blockade of S1P production or S1PR3 activity under normal conditions induces mechanical hyposensitivity and under inflammatory conditions returns mechanical sensitivity to normal levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological blockade data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Baseline levels of S1P are necessary and sufficient for setting normal mechanical pain thresholds.
source: While previous studies have shown that elevated S1P triggers acute pain and injury-evoked thermal sensitization (Mair et al., 2011; Camprubí-Robles et al., 2013), we now demonstrate that baseline levels of S1P are necessary and sufficient for setting normal mechanical pain thresholds.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral and electrophysiological data and cited references.

claim: Elevated S1P selectively triggers thermal sensitization via activation of TRPV1+ heat nociceptors, with no effect on mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: By contrast, elevated S1P selectively triggers thermal sensitization via activation of TRPV1+ heat nociceptors, with no effect on mechanical hypersensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Constitutive S1P signaling plays an essential role in mechanical pain.
source: Our findings uncover an essential role for constitutive S1P signaling in mechanical pain.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: S1P constitutively enhances the excitability of A mechanonociceptors (AMs) via closure of KCNQ2/3 potassium channels to tune mechanical pain sensitivity.
source: We show that S1P constitutively enhances the excitability of A mechanonociceptors (AMs) via closure of KCNQ2/3 potassium channels to tune mechanical pain sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The effects of S1P are completely dependent on S1PR3.
source: The effects of S1P are completely dependent on S1PR3.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from S1PR3 KO mice and pharmacological blockade experiments.

claim: S1PR3 is a selective role for acute mechanical pain.
source: These results demonstrate a selective role for S1PR3 in acute mechanical pain.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1.

claim: S1PR3 signaling sets mechanical pain sensitivity.
source: Overall, these data show that S1PR3 signaling sets mechanical pain sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by behavioral and pharmacological data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Constitutive activation of S1PR3 by S1P is required for normal mechanosensitivity.
source: These data show that constitutive activation of S1PR3 by S1P is required for normal mechanosensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Baseline S1P levels are sufficient to maximally exert their effect on S1PR3-dependent mechanical pain.
source: Our data establish that baseline S1P levels are sufficient to maximally exert their effect on S1PR3-dependent mechanical pain, such that increased S1P does not evoke mechanical hypersensitivity, but diminished S1P leads to mechanical hyposensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Increased S1P does not evoke mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: Our data establish that baseline S1P levels are sufficient to maximally exert their effect on S1PR3-dependent mechanical pain, such that increased S1P does not evoke mechanical hypersensitivity, but diminished S1P leads to mechanical hyposensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Diminished S1P leads to mechanical hyposensitivity.
source: Our data establish that baseline S1P levels are sufficient to maximally exert their effect on S1PR3-dependent mechanical pain, such that increased S1P does not evoke mechanical hypersensitivity, but diminished S1P leads to mechanical hyposensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Baseline S1P/S1PR3 signaling governs mechanical pain thresholds through modulation of KCNQ2/3 channel activity in AM neurons.
source: In summary, our electrophysiological and behavioral observations support a model in which baseline S1P/S1PR3 signaling governs mechanical pain thresholds through modulation of KCNQ2/3 channel activity in AM neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: GPCR-mediated inhibition of KCNQ2/3 potassium channels is a well-known mechanism by which neuronal excitability is regulated.
source: GPCR-mediated inhibition of KCNQ2/3 potassium channels is a well-known mechanism by which neuronal excitability is regulated (Passmore et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: KCNQ channels are required for normal mechanonociceptive responses in dorsal horn neurons receiving Aδ input.
source: Other studies have shown that KCNQ channels mediate excitability of Aδ fibers (Schütze et al., 2016; Passmore et al., 2012) and are required for normal mechanonociceptive responses in dorsal horn neurons receiving Aδ input (Passmore et al., 2012), and that opening KCNQ2/3 channels directly with retigabine alleviates pain in vivo (Xu et al., 2010; Hayashi et al., 2014; Blackburn-Munro and Jensen, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.
